title: Combining low-density cell culture, single-cell tracking, and patch-clamp to monitor the behavior of postnatal murine cerebellar neural stem cells
protocol: Dilute the poly-l-lysine in sterile water from the stock solution (0.1 mg/mL) to a final concentration of 10 μg/mL.
Add the appropriate amount of diluted poly-l-lysine to the culture surface; typically 1 ml per 25 cm² is required under sterile conditions.
Cover and incubate at 37°C for 1–2 h.
Remove the solution by aspiration and thoroughly rinse the surface with sterile water.
Cover and allow to dry at room temperature for at least 1 h.
Sacrifice P0 mice in accordance with current regulatory guidelines and using protocols approved by the institution.
Euthanize the mouse pup by decapitation, separate the head from the body, and wipe the head of the pup with 70% ethanol.
Place the embryo’s head in a 60 mm Petri dish with cold Neurobasal (NB) medium.
Hold the head with stainless forceps to see the back of the skull clearly.
Insert microdissection scissors into the foramen magnum and cut straight toward the eyes.
Peel away the skin of the head using curved forceps to expose the brain.
Lift the skull gently with curved forceps to expose the brain without cutting through it.
Pinch off the cerebellum and transfer it to a 35 mm Petri dish with EBSS medium.
Gently remove the meninges from the cerebellum using one 30G syringe needle.
Fix the cerebellum to the dish using another 30G syringe needle.
Remove all EBSS medium from the dish using a Pasteur pipette.
Add papain solution to the tissue in the dish.
Chop up the tissue with a surgical blade.
Incubate for 45 minutes at 37°C in 5% CO2 in sterile conditions.
Transfer pieces of cerebellum to a 15 mL conical tube using a siliconized Pasteur pipette.
Mechanically dissociate the tissue by pipetting up and down until the lysate is homogeneous.
Centrifuge the mixture at 200 ×g for 5 minutes at room temperature.
Prepare re-suspension medium by mixing EBSS, reconstituted albumin-ovomucoid inhibitor, DNase solution, and APV in a 15 mL conical tube.
Remove the supernatant after centrifugation.
Resuspend the cell pellet in the prepared re-suspension medium using a siliconized Pasteur pipette.
Prepare a discontinuous density gradient by carefully layering the resuspended cell suspension on top of albumin-ovomucoid inhibitor.
Centrifuge at 200 ×g for 5 min at room temperature (RT).
Remove the supernatant and resuspend the pellet in 2 ml of NB medium.
Count the number of viable cells by mixing 50 μL of Trypan blue, 40 μL of NB medium, and 10 μL of cell suspension in a tube.
Place 10 μL of this mixture into a hemocytometer.
Plate the cells at low density (50,000 cells/cm²) in NB medium supplemented with 2% B27, 100 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, amphotericin 0.25 μg/mL, and L-glutamine 0.5 mM.
Power up the computer, CO₂ and temperature control systems, the microscope, and the hardware for live time-lapse video-microscopy imaging.
Adjust the temperature to 37°C and the CO₂ level to 5%.
Wait 1–2 hours for the CO₂ and temperature levels to stabilize.
Make a small mark on the bottom of a well that does not contain cells.
Place the culture plate in the microscope chamber.
Tightly fix the plate to the microscope to prevent any movement during the video-microscopy experiment.
Wait 20 min until the temperature of the cell culture medium has equilibrated in the chamber.
Run the software and set up the time-lapse experiment.
Select the length of the experiment and the image acquisition cycles.
Use cycles of 5 min, typically lasting 4 or 5 days.
Determine the frequency necessary to avoid phototoxicity-induced cell death.
Search for the mark made previously in the plate.
Define it as the reference point (position 1, equivalent to xyz zero coordinates).
Take a photo of the zero position to reset coordinates if necessary.
Select the rest of the positions (x and y coordinates) and adjust focus (z coordinate) for each position.
Choose the type of acquisition and exposure time in the wavelength selection tab menu.
In experiments, only select brightfield with an exposure time of 10–50 ms.
Close shutters for transmitted light and epifluorescence between cycles and positions to avoid toxicity induced by light exposure.
Name the experiment and the folder where data will be stored.
Save the list of positions.
Click on the “run now” button to start the experiment.
Pause the experiment once a day if necessary to re-adjust the focus conditions using the “overwrite z button”.
If the medium needs to be changed, pause the experiment and take the plate out of the chamber.
Change the medium under sterile conditions and put the plate back into the chamber (see step 21).
Re-adjust the focus and continue with the experiment.
After finishing the experiment, click the “finish” button and remove the plate.
Remove the medium from the wells.
Add 500 μL of sterile Phosphate Buffered Saline (PBS) to wash the cells.
Repeat washing the cells twice with PBS.
Add 500 μL of 4% (wt/vol) paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS and fix the cells at RT for 10 min.
Wash the cells three times with 500 μL of sterile PBS.
Add 500 μL per well of a blocking solution containing 2% (wt/vol) BSA and 0.2% (vol/vol) Triton X-100 in PBS.
Incubate for 1 h at RT.
Remove the blocking solution.
Add 200–400 μL of primary antibody solution containing diluted GFAP, βIII-tubulin, SOX2, VGLUT1, and VGAT antibodies to the wells.
Incubate for 18 hours at 4°C.
Remove the primary antibody solution and wash the wells three times with PBS (5 minutes each).
Add 200–400 μL of secondary antibody solution containing diluted Anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L) 594, Anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L) 488, Anti-Mouse IgG2b 488, and Anti-Mouse IgG1 to the wells.
Incubate for 1–2 hours at room temperature in the dark.
Wash three times with PBS (5 minutes each).
For VGAT signal amplification, incubate for 1–2 hours at room temperature in the dark with diluted biotin Anti-Mouse secondary antibody.
Perform a wash step with PBS as previously described.
Incubate for 1 hour at room temperature in the dark with Streptavidin 594 diluted in blocking solution.
Repeat the wash step with PBS.
Maintain cells in 1 mL of PBS prior to next steps.
Optionally, remove PBS and add two drops of Aqua-Poly/Mount aqueous mounting medium.
Place the plate back into the microscope chamber and secure tightly.
Reload the zero position using the indication made previously.
Re-set the rest of the positions to this reference point by clicking the “Offset All X, Y, Z” button.
Re-set the focal distance (z coordinate).
Wait around 20 minutes for the temperature of the plate to equilibrate in the chamber.
Configure conditions for fluorescence emission in the “wavelength tab menu”.
Obtain a final round of images.
Adjust the fluorescence exposure to acquire the best quality images.
Save the data and export using the software’s file/export to Tagged Image File Format (Tiff) option.
Rename the image channels: For brightfield images, change c1 to c0; for FITC images, change it to c2; for CY3 images, change to c3; for CY5 images, change to c4.
Convert the images to a PNG format.
Start the “tTt Converter tool” software.
Define the input and output folder in the tTt Converter tool.
Specify the markers used for each of the channels (c), positions (xy), and time-points (t) in the tTt Converter tool.
Click the “convert images" button in the tTt Converter tool.
Select the wavelength that corresponds to the brightfield image.
Click twice on the position to be tracked in the "Cell Editor Window".
Adjust the contrast and brightness as needed.
Press the F2 key to start tracking.
Situating the mouse pointer on the cell, press the “0” key during tracking for specific events.
Record cell events such as division, apoptosis or loss in the “Cell Editor Window”.
Match brightfield images with immunofluorescence images to define cell progeny nature.
Save the experiment once all positions are tracked.
Export cell data and lineage tree through the "Export menu" to the tTt export folder.
Make the patch-clamp recording pipettes for the day.
Pull glass electrodes using a two-step pipette puller, adjusting settings to achieve resistance of about 4 MΩ.
Polish the pipette’s tip with a microforge to increase resistance to 4.5–5 MΩ.
Make drug application pipettes similarly.
Place pipettes in a closed container to prevent soiling by airborne dust.
Thaw an aliquot of the internal solution.
Keep the thawed solution on ice, protected from light.
Prepare dilutions of stock drug solutions in external solution.
Switch on all apparatus required for the experiment.
Run PATCHMASTER software for cell stimulation and data acquisition.
Open a new experiment in the program’s menu.
Feed the gravity-driven perfusion line with external solution.
Check for air bubbles in the perfusion line.
Flush the perfusion line and recording chamber with ddH2O at the end of each day to avoid bacterial contamination.
If lipophilic compounds are used, rinse pipelines with ethanol before washing them with ddH2O.
Transfer a poly-l-lysine coated coverslip loaded with cells to the recording chamber using straight forceps.
Connect the ground electrode to the head stage of the patch-clamp amplifier.
Secure the plate in the recording chamber.
Start perfusion of the external solution at a rate of 1 mL/min.
Turn on the vacuum aspiration to remove the solution from the recording chamber through an outlet connected to an Erlenmeyer container.
Check that the liquid level in the recording chamber stays above the cell’s plane.
Use a low power objective (10×) and move the stage of the microscope to situate some cells in the center of the field of view.
Dip the pipette tip into a 1 mL Eppendorf tube with the external solution containing the drug for a few seconds such that the solution enters the pipette by capillarity.
Use a needle attached to a 2 mL syringe to backfill the pipette with the same solution.
Remove any air bubbles from the pipette’s interior by shaking the pipette as if it were an old mercury thermometer.
Fit the drug application pipette to a pipette holder and use a micromanipulator to orientate the pipette towards the recording chamber.
Fill a recording pipette with a filtered internal solution to 60%–75% of capacity.
Intercalate a 0.22 μm filter between the syringe and the needle.
Insert the glass-pipette into the electrode holder so that the chlorinated electrode is placed into the internal solution.
Secure the pipette in the holder.
Activate the “SET-UP” mode in the PATCHMASTER.
Set the amplifier gain to 5 mV/pA.
Set digital oscilloscope gain and time resolution depending on the expected response size.
Set the capacitance cancellation and series resistance compensation to 0.
Set the current filter bandwidth to 2.9 Hz.
Set the test pulse parameters to 5 mV for 5 ms every 30 ms from a holding potential of 0 mV.
Set the baseline correction to 0.
Lower the recording electrode into the bath using a micromanipulator.
Visualize the pipette current offset and the current response to test pulses in the oscilloscope screen.
Adjust the current offset to zero in the amplifier.
Move the pipette tip into the field of view under a 10× objective.
Exchange the 10× objective for an objective with higher magnification (63×).
Focus on the plane immediately above the cell of interest.
Lower the pipette until its tip can be clearly seen.
Focus the cell and capture an image of it.
Apply test pulses continuously while bringing the electrode tip close to the cell membrane.
Press the electrode tip up against the cell membrane.
Start applying negative pressure inside the pipette through a side port connected to a 10 mL syringe by a silicone tube.
Monitor the reduction in current amplitude due to increased pipette resistance.
Gradually adjust the holding potential to negative values up to −70 mV at ≈3 s intervals (−10 mV, −20 mV, −30 mV, ...).
Monitor the formation of a seal with high mechanical and electrical resistance between the pipette tip and the plasma membrane.
Increase pipette resistance to a minimum of 1 GΩ.
Apply negative pressure and wait for the formation of a giga-seal upon contact with the cell.
Monitor current reduction to values close to 0 pA during voltage pulse application, indicating a cell-attached configuration has been achieved.
Cancel pipette capacitive transients upon giga-seal formation by adjusting amplifier gain or oscilloscope screen settings.
Set the holding voltage to −70 mV.
Apply brief, intense negative pressure pulses to break open the membrane patch enclosed in the pipette.
Cancel the cell capacitive transients due to the charging/discharging of the membrane capacitor.
Adjust the amplifier gain and oscilloscope screen parameters to the expected recording conditions.
Wait several minutes to complete cell dialysis with the internal solution while monitoring leak current amplitude and series resistance for stability and voltage-clamp suitability.
Configure a stimulation protocol for the cell under study.
Apply step depolarizations, such as a 100 ms pulse to +10 mV, to activate voltage-gated ion channels.
Record and store the currents produced in response to voltage-stimulation.
Include the "P/n" procedure to subtract leak and capacitive currents from recorded data.
Trigger small voltage pulses that do not activate ion channels to measure leak and capacitive currents.
Scale the measured leak and capacitive currents to match the amplitude of test pulse currents.
Subtract scaled leak and capacitive currents from current responses evoked by test pulses.
Isolate voltage-activated ion currents by subtracting background currents.
Carefully bring the pipette close (5–15 μm) to the cell being recorded.
Monitor the holding (leak) current as an indicator of seal integrity.
Clear external solution from the pipette tip by applying several pressure pulses when it is far from the cell under study.
Apply a pulse of pressure to the interior of the application pipette to deliver the drug (1 mM glutamate, 100 μM GABA or 100 μM 5-HT) used to activate ionotropic receptors.
Record and store the currents produced in response to agonist-stimulation for subsequent analysis and display.
Sustain drug application for the time needed to produce a clear response and its eventual decline.
Cease the application and washout the drug by perfusion of the external solution.
Once the membrane current recovers to baseline, apply a second drug from a different pipette.
In cells with a leak current of a few pA at a voltage close to the resting membrane potential, switch from the voltage-clamp to the current-clamp mode.
Record the resting potential (when Ip = 0 pA).
Assess changes in membrane potential when current is injected, such as a step of +75 pA for 250 ms.
Administer a receptor agonist, such as 100 μM 5-HT, to observe depolarizing responses and action potentials if applicable.
Discard cells with a leak current larger than -100 pA during recordings.
Record synaptic currents evoked by transmitters released from a cell making a synaptic contact with the recorded cell.
Apply 5-HT (100 μM) to an unclamped bipolar cell to elicit glutamate release.
Start local application of MK-801 (10 μM), a NMDA antagonist, to reduce current amplitudes and identify responsible receptors.
Recognize synaptic-like currents by their rapid onset and brief duration.
Stop recording after the experiment is completed.
Save the recorded file.
Pull the recording pipette away from the cell.
Lift the electrode out of the bath.
Remove the glass pipette from the electrode holder.
